The dimensions of contrast: size/scale, value/tone, color/hue, shape, texture, direction, and type
Contrast as the primary tool for emphasis and for guiding attention to a focal point

claims.claim: Contrast is a visual difference between paired elements that increases the distinct character of each, adds energy and visual range to a composition, and lets a viewer distinguish one object by comparing it against another.
No design relies on only one kind of contrast, but usually one kind dominates; and as contrast between elements diminishes, the elements feel similar and visual interest decreases.

Contrast can be created across multiple dimensions, including color, size, and shape, and for text through varied colors, serif versus sans serif, unusual type pairings, or type used in place of an image; Johannes Itten of the Bauhaus catalogued pairings such as large/small, thick/thin, light/heavy, straight/curved, and light/dark.

Emphasis is achieved by making one element gain the eye's attention, creating a single focal point that the eye reaches before the rest of the composition; contrast is one of the principles designers use to support this, and emphasis is strongly linked to visual hierarchy.

Low-contrast text harms readability, causes eye strain, and disproportionately affects older adults, people with vision impairments (such as presbyopia, macular degeneration, glaucoma, and cataracts), and users reading in bright light or glare.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), published by the W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, define specific minimum contrast ratios for text under Success Criterion 1.4.3 at conformance level AA: at least 4.5:1 for normal text and at least 3:1 for large text.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many named 'types' of contrast exist.
positions: General design texts list broad perceptual dimensions (size, value, color, shape, texture, direction, type).
Itten's color theory enumerates seven specific color contrasts (hue, light-dark, cold-warm, complementary, simultaneous, saturation, extension).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the broad perceptual dimensions as the framework and treats color as one dimension. Itten's seven color contrasts are color-theory material and are only referenced, not enumerated, keeping color harmony within the Color Theory topic.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('a concept students use to organize information', 'name the concept, describe its parts') with no substantive claims about contrast; none of it was usable as evidence.
